correctness.rationale: The published expansion at r=2 and preperiod criterion at odd prime powers match the hypotheses and indices. An independent derivation is in /workspace/branches/preperiod-proof-check.md: split the finite exponential expansion into unit and nonunit frequencies; the latter give, for n≥1, a unit times p^n E_n modulo p^r and a nonzero discrepancy at n=0. This also verifies s≥1 and the interpretation using the least eventual period. For n≥2 the unit terms at modulus p² obey the affine shift since ((ia)^d−1)^2=0; the first difference is divisible by p directly from the unit frequencies (not from the affine shape alone). An independent bounded modular EGF recurrence replay through 3d+9 gave the six 43-adic zero classes and eight 433-adic classes in RESULT.md, including wrap-around; it found only the stated adjacent pairs and no cyclic triple. The 43-adic square checks at indices (12,96) and (54,138) give affine pairs (32,29) and (18,14) modulo 43 with roots 33 and 11; r≡2786 or 980 (mod 3612), exactly the single progression starting at 980 with step 1806. At 433, the check at (214,646) gives (88,317) modulo 433 with root 165, hence r=71496+187056j. The shift law propagates beyond all tested indices; the finite replay is not by itself an infinite proof. E_0=E_1=1 and s≥1 settle the small exponents and the zero-index exception. Both supplied evidence files were read, and the frozen script was not executed. The separate cited Question 5.1 wording was not independently verifiable; this does not enter the proof of the spectra.

value.rationale: These primes are motivated by actual adjacent-zero pairs and a known double defect at 43, not arbitrary small parameters. An exact phase diagram determines every defect and the first exceptional exponent at 433 without scanning up to that exponent or manipulating numbers modulo the corresponding giant prime powers. The split-to-half-period mechanism at 43 explains the structure of a progression rather than merely extending a table. This resolves the concrete progression mathematically; no significance for all primes is inferred.
